podcast.title: Solo Work After Rage Against the Machine (Fall 2000)
podcast.body: After his departure from Rage Against the Machine in the fall of 2000, Zack de la Rocha pursued solo work, collaborating with producers like DJ Shadow and Dan The Automator, and later Trent Reznor. Despite these efforts, he struggled to complete a full album, often feeling uninspired. "When Zach De La Roca left Raging Against the Machine in the fall of 2000, it was almost a given that he would move on to some kind of solo work. He did. But then he kind of got lost. He worked with a series of DJ slash producers like DJ Shadow and Dan The Automator."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Awareness of Racism
podcast.body: As the only Latino child in his class, Dela Roka developed an acute awareness of casual racism, an experience that strongly influenced his determination to speak out against injustice. "as the only Latino kid in his class, he was acutely aware of all kinds of casual racism, and he became determined to speak out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Controversial Stance on George W. Bush (Unspecified Year)
podcast.body: The band's vocalist, Zack de la Rocha, faced potential legal repercussions after media reports claimed he had expressed a desire for US President George W. Bush's assassination. While he didn't explicitly call for his death, he unequivocally stated that Bush was a war criminal deserving of trial and execution by hanging for crimes against humanity stemming from the Afghanistan wars. He publicly refused to retract these statements, leading to widespread controversy and censorship. "Él había dicho una entrevista que estaba deseando que matase a George Bush, presidente de los Estados Unidos...realmente lo que había dicho es que George Bush por las guerras afganistán era en el fondo un criminal de guerra que debería haber sido judrado y posteriormente orcado por crímenes contra la humanidad y de hecho no se retractó de ninguna de sus palabras y acabo siendo normalmente censurado."

podcast.title: Departure from Rage Against The Machine
podcast.body: De la Rocha left Rage Against The Machine due to a "creative dispute, maybe a political dispute," as he wished to pursue a musical direction that diverged from the other band members' vision. "he left the band over a creative dispute, maybe a political dispute. He wanted to take the band in one direction while the other guys didn't want to go there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discovery of Freestyle Rapping
podcast.body: Tom Morello first encountered Zach Dela Roka at a club where Dela Roka was practicing his freestyle rapping. Impressed by what he heard, Morello initiated a conversation that ultimately led to their collaboration and the formation of Rage Against The Machine. "One night, Tom was out at a club where Zach happened to be working on his freestyle rapping."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Life and Family
podcast.body: Born in Long Beach, California, Zach Dela Roka experienced a fractured family life, being shuttled between his parents. His father was an artist with extreme artistic and religious views who suffered a nervous breakdown, leading him to destroy all his paintings and demand Zach's help in burning them. His mother was in the process of completing her PhD in anthropology. "He was born in Long Beach, California, and he came from a broken family."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Beginnings
podcast.body: Dela Roka started playing guitar at the age of eight. By his teenage years, he was deeply engrossed in punk music, citing bands like The Clash, Minor Threat, Bad Brains, and Bad Religion as significant influences. "He picked up a guitar at eight, and by the time he was a teenager, Zach was deep into punk, clash, minor threat, bad brains, bad religion, that kind of thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Patti Smith Hall of Fame Inductor
podcast.body: Zach De La Rocha inducted Patti Smith into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2007. He delivered a speech praising her for disrupting a "too slick" rock scene with her "literate yet street savvy lyrics" that confronted various topics. "When Paddy Smith was inducted into the Rock Hall in 2007 by a Zach De La Roca from Rage Against the Machine, he said, Rock was getting too slick for its own good when Paddy Smith burst on the scene and tore it apart."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Solo Album with Trent Reznor - Unreleased
podcast.body: After Rage Against the Machine disbanded in 2000, Zack De La Rocha began working on a solo record, delving into hip hop and freestyle rapping. He collaborated with DJ Shadow, Dan the Automator, and Trent Reznor, who produced the material. Despite the material being considered "good" by Reznor, the album was never released and was shelved indefinitely for unknown reasons. "Rage was done by 2000... But Zach was determined to go solo. He got deep into hip hop and freestyle rapping and started working with DJ Shadow, Dan the Automator, and Trent Rosner on a solo record. The material was good too, according to Trent anyway. But for a recent still unknown, the album was never released, shelved forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Struggles with Solo Direction
podcast.body: According to Trent Reznor, de la Rocha faced difficulty in deciding on a clear musical direction for his solo work, coupled with the pressure of making an "important statement" after leaving "one of the best bands of the 90s." "Over time I think it was a matter of Zach not knowing what direction to go. I know the feeling of fear he's in a difficult position of leaving one of the best bands of the 90s, and he wants to make an important statement when he makes it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Uninspired by Trent Reznor Collaboration
podcast.body: Although Trent Reznor felt their collaboration "went well" and produced around 20 tracks, Zack de la Rocha expressed in interviews that he was "just going through the motions" and felt "uninspired by the whole experience." This lack of enthusiasm from de la Rocha contributed to the project ultimately remaining unreleased. "Well, in interviews, Zach said he was just going through the motions and was uninspired by the whole experience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unreleased Album with Trent Reznor
podcast.body: De la Rocha worked on a solo album with Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails, reportedly recording up to 20 songs. However, Reznor stated that "that album will never see the light of day" due to de la Rocha's indecision about the musical direction and his desire to make an important statement after leaving a prominent band. "I know for a fact that he worked on an album with Trent Resner of Nineteen Snails. There may have been up to 20 songs recorded for this CD, but as Trent told me directly, and I quote, that album will never see the light of day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Implosion (October 18, 2000) – Zack de la Rocha's Departure
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine experienced an "implosion" on October 18, 2000, when their singer, Zack de la Rocha, quit the band. Despite this, the remaining three members—Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, and Brad Wilk—decided to stay together and search for a new vocalist, leading to the formation of Audioslave. "Singer and Zacti La Roca quit the band on October 18, 2000, and frankly, that was fine as far as the other three guys were concerned. They planned to stay together."

xref.title: Zack de la Rocha Quits (2000)
xref.body: On October 18, 2000, Zack de la Rocha quit the band, citing a "completely failed" decision-making process that "no longer meaning the aspirations of all four of us collectively as a band, and from my perspective has undermined our artistic and political ideal." This was broadly understood as political and creative differences, which extended to minor disputes like the color of merchandise t-shirts. "It was necessary to leave Rage because our decision-making process has completely failed."

xref.title: Zack de la Rocha's Departure and Return (2000, 2007)
xref.body: Zack de la Rocha left Rage Against the Machine in the fall of 2000 to pursue solo work, but faced challenges finding inspiration for a full album. The band later reunited in 2007 and has continued to perform through a series of live gigs, demonstrating their enduring presence despite de la Rocha's earlier departure. "When Zach De La Roca left Raging Against the Machine in the fall of 2000, it was almost a given that he would move on to some kind of solo work. He did. But then he kind of got lost. It all worked out well, though. Rage got back to you there in 2007 and had been holding it together through a series of live gigs ever since."

xref.title: Search for New Vocalist (2001)

B-Real of Cypress Hill tried out, but was deemed too similar to Zack de la Rocha, and the band thought they might not want a rapper. "It is true, however, that be real of Cypress Hill tried out. He sounded a little too much like Zach."

xref.title: "Evil Empire" Cover Art Interpretation
xref.body: Zack de la Rocha of Rage Against the Machine provided an interpretation of the boy's expression on the "Evil Empire" album cover, a painting by Mel Ramos. He stated that the boy's smile is a facade, projecting control within the power structure of the United States, but upon deeper examination, the boy is actually "very, very afraid." "Zach D'Auroraka says it's all about the power structure in the United States. He's smiling because he wants to project that he's in control."

xref.title: Audioslave Formed After Rick Rubin Suggested Chris Cornell; Be Real of Cypress Hill Also Auditioned
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha quit Rage Against the Machine in 2000, the remaining three members tried to continue under the RATM name with a new singer. Be Real of Cypress Hill auditioned. But after some jamming, they decided they didn't want a Zack sound-alike — they wanted something new. Producer Rick Rubin suggested they talk to ex-Soundgarden singer Chris Cornell. The chemistry was immediate. They began writing as "Civilian" or "the Civilian project" but had to rename when they discovered another group was using that name. They chose Audioslave. The group was essentially Rage with a different singer, and they were productive from 2001 through 2007. "The chemistry was immediate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Audition for Rage Against the Machine – Rick Rubin's Suggestion
xref.body: After his solo album's disappointing sales, and with Rage Against the Machine's singer Zack de la Rocha having quit, producer Rick Rubin suggested Chris Cornell as a potential new vocalist for the remaining members. The chemistry between Cornell and the instrumentalists was instantaneous, leading them to write 21 songs in just 19 days. "Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell. The chemistry was so instant that they wrote 21 songs in just 19 days."

xref.title: Collaboration with Zack de la Rocha
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha left Rage Against the Machine in 2000, he embarked on a collaboration with Trent Reznor, which was rumored to have produced up to 20 tracks. Although the project went well from Reznor's perspective, it was ultimately never released, with Reznor stating it "will never see a light of day," a sentiment echoed by de la Rocha who felt uninspired. "I was doing some other musical projects, none of which kind of panned out. And then the tapeworm thing didn't turn out the way we'd hoped. Worked on Zach's Aote Delroge's record. And that went well, but that's never going to see a lighted Aote thing."

xref.title: Dreadlocks in 1990s Rock and Metal
xref.body: Zack de la Rocha, from Rage Against the Machine, was one of the prominent figures in the 1990s music scene to adopt dreadlocks, showcasing the style's widespread appeal across genres. "And then through the 90s, dreads appeared on everyone from Rob Zombie and Zach from Raging Us the Machine to Jonathan Davis of Corn."

xref.title: Formation from Rage Against The Machine Members
xref.body: This band was formed when Chris Cornell joined the remaining three members of Rage Against The Machine (Tom Morello, Timmy, and Brad) after their singer Zack de la Rocha left. The group decided to change their name from Rage Against The Machine to Audioslave. "Tom Morello on the line. And I'm not really sure why there was a collective decision to jettison the Rage name in favor of Audio Slive, which is where we are today."

xref.body: Audioslave formed when the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) sought a new singer after Zack de la Rocha's departure. Producer Rick Rubin suggested Chris Cornell, leading to an instant creative connection and the rapid composition of 21 songs. "Rage Against the Machine had imploded... xref.title: Joining Rage Against The Machine (unofficially)
xref.body: Cornell was contacted by Tom Morello after Zack de la Rocha left Rage Against The Machine. He joined Morello, Timmy, and Brad, and they convened to write songs, which "worked out really well." A bootleg recording from this period exists, labeled "Rage Against The Machine, both Chris Cornell and Vocals. Tom Morello on the line." "Now Chris thought this sounded pretty good, so they convened to write some songs. That worked out really well. And Chris joined Rage Against The Machine."

xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha's departure, the remaining three members wanted to stay together. They briefly considered becoming the backing band for Ozzy Osbourne or working with Macy Gray. xref.title: Powerful Bottom End
xref.body: A key element contributing to Rage Against the Machine's distinct sound was their powerful "bottom end," driven by bassist Tim Commerford and drummer Brad Wilk. Singer Zack de la Rocha and guitarist Tom Morello recognized the need to allow the rhythm section ample space to contribute to the band's overall sound. "One of the things that made Rage Against the Machine so cool was that bottom end."

xref.title: Rage Against the Machine Iteration
xref.body: Prophets of Rage is considered another iteration of Rage Against the Machine, featuring its instrumental members alongside Chuck D of Public Enemy and B-Real of Cypress Hill, effectively replacing Zack de la Rocha. "And then there's Prophets of Rage, of course, which could be looked at as yet another iteration of Rage Against the Machine with Chuck D and B. Real and place him Zach."

xref.title: Tim Commerford's Background and Influences
xref.body: Tim Commerford, known by various names including Tim Bob and Tim C, grew up in Irvine, south of Los Angeles. His mother was a mathematician and his father an aeronautical engineer who worked on the space shuttle. He and Zack de la Rocha formed their first band, Juvenile Expression, in grade seven, after Zack taught Tim to play bass using the Sex Pistols' "Never Mind the Bollocks" album. Tim also spent hours learning Geddy Lee's bass parts from Rush albums. "Mom was a mathematician while his dad was an aeronautical engineer who actually worked on the space shuttle."

xref.title: Vocal Style Development
xref.body: Ben, the vocalist, initially spent the first five years of the band trying to emulate other singers like Eddie Vedder, Scott Weiland, and Zack de la Rocha. He eventually realized he couldn't sound like them and developed his own distinctive style. This unique vocal approach, combined with Ian's guitar playing, helped the band stand out from other Canadian bands of the era like Moist, Treble Charger, and The Tea Party. "I, the first five years of being in a band, you know, I was trying to sound like other people, you know, I was trying to sound like Eddie Vetter. I was trying to sound like Scott Watt. I'm trying to sound like Zack Delroch. You know, like, I'm trying to do that. And then I realized I can't do that, you know, so I just kind of ended up being me."

xref.body: While all members of Rage Against the Machine were political activists, singer Zack de la Rocha was "exponentially more passionate" in that direction, which contributed to internal differences.
